html:
By tradition, Buddhism reached the Chinese court in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han, who founded the White Horse Temple at Luoyang in 68 CE, the first Buddhist temple in China.

The story goes that the emperor dreamed of a golden figure flying, and his advisers told him it was the Buddha of the west. He sent envoys, who came back with two Indian monks carrying scriptures on white horses; the temple was named after them.

In truth Buddhism probably arrived more slowly, with merchants and monks travelling the Silk Road from Central Asia, where the Kushan Empire ruled. A brother of Emperor Ming was already honouring the Buddha in 65 CE. Translators such as An Shigao, a Parthian prince who came to Luoyang around 148, put the first scriptures into Chinese. Buddhism grew slowly under the Han and spread fast in the troubled centuries after. From China it passed on to Korea and Japan.
sum: By tradition, Buddhism reached the Chinese court in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han, who founded the White Horse Temple at Luoyang in 68 CE, the first Buddhist temple in China.
